paragraphs.text: A cake of ripe pu’er from Yunnan leaf, made in 1998 and sold under the [Zhong Cha mark](zhong-cha-pai:definition), the brand of the China National Tea Corporation. The mark names who sold the tea, not how fine the leaf is. From the late 1980s the larger factories moved to their own names and newer, smaller makers took up the label, so on a cake from this decade the year of making says more than the wrapper does.

Leaf for [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) is heaped warm and damp in a [fermenting pile](shou:wet-piling) before it is pressed. Yunnan’s factories brought that method into production in 1973, which puts 1998 in the style’s third decade. At twenty-eight years this cake is well past the ten years the trade counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf keeps changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, so storage has shaped it as much as the years have.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
